research.label: Research target alignment
research.method: For each configured criterion, q = number of requested tags documented at the site / number of unique requested tags. Index = 100 × weighted mean q.
assumptions: This index measures alignment with the user's stated geological targets, not scientific value, discovery likelihood or sample accessibility.
Tags are qualitative literature descriptions over the recorded region; an unreported target is not proof of physical absence.
Materials and landforms may overlap conceptually; their weights are user preferences, not independent probabilities.

rover_field_test.label: Regional rover test fit
rover_field_test.method: q = max(0, 1 − |measured regional value − user target| / user tolerance). Index = 100 × weighted mean q.
assumptions: Target 1 degree with tolerance 5 degrees and target relief 100 m with tolerance 300 m are editable example preferences, not validated rover operating limits.
Both terrain metrics use roughly 3.7 km cells. They cannot resolve rocks, metre-scale slopes, trafficability or wheel–soil interactions.
The index measures regional environment fit for planning a test, not vehicle performance or safety.

analog_reference.label: Similarity to {mars_name} (Mars)
analog_reference.method: Similarity = 100 / (1 + D), where D is the weighted mean of per-feature distances between each Earth site and {mars_name}: regional slope and relief (scaled differences at the same ~3.7 km baseline), landforms and minerals (Jaccard distance of literature tags) and dryness (precipitation difference). This is the same calculation as Explore's analog ranking (spec {analog_version}). Each factor's points show how much of the 100 it cost.
assumptions: The Mars site is the one paired with your mission in Mission Design.

Slope and relief together keep the analog spec's terrain share; the Earth Low slopes and Less rugged ground sliders only set the split between them. Landforms, minerals and dryness keep the analog spec weights.
Elevation and sunlight are not compared: elevations use different datums on the two planets, and Mars receives 0.431 of Earth's sunlight (NASA Mars Fact Sheet).
Terrain metrics use roughly 3.7 km cells on both planets; they cannot resolve rocks, metre-scale slopes or trafficability. Landform and mineral tags are literature labels, not spectral measurements.
The index is a heuristic similarity, not a probability or a validated test-site rating.

base_planning.label: Base-planning evidence review
base_planning.method: No aggregate score: essential infrastructure, resource and hazard evidence is not available.
assumptions: Terrain profiles alone cannot establish base viability.
evidence_gaps: Reliable water/resource quantities and extraction feasibility
Seasonal surface power and energy-storage requirements
Geotechnical bearing capacity and landing-scale hazards
